Entertainment.title: Chris Brown: US singer pleads guilty to affray over 'vicious' nightclub attack in London
Entertainment.text:
US singer Chris Brown has pleaded guilty to affray over what prosecutors called "a vicious and unprovoked attack" in a London nightclub in 2023.

Police said CCTV showed that Brown, one of the world's biggest R&B stars, hit the victim on the head with a glass bottle several times, and that the man was then chased, pushed to the floor and kicked.

The 37-year-old star had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied - assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon, namely a tequila bottle. However, those charges have now been dropped.

Affray, which is defined as using or threatening violence towards someone and making them fear for their safety, is punishable by up to three years in jail. Brown will be sentenced in October.

Brown's vocal coach, 40-year-old Omololu Akinlolu, a rapper from Florida who performs under the name Hoody Baby, also pleaded guilty to affray and had assault and attempted grievous bodily harm charges dropped.

Det Con Zara Ripamonti of the Metropolitan Police said: "This was a disgraceful, unprovoked assault that put a man in hospital.

"There is no place for serious violence like this in the London and I'm pleased these men accepted what they did wasn't just completely unacceptable - but criminal.

"This has been a long investigation and we've worked with police colleagues in the UK to bring these two men to justice."

The attack happened at the Tape venue, a private members' club in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Prosecutors said Brown approached the victim from the dance floor then struck him over the head with a bottle, and Akinlolu joined Brown and punched the victim in the head.

"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."

The victim, music producer Abe Diaw, needed hospital treatment for head and knee injuries.

Claire Campbell, senior crown prosecutor in CPS London South, said: "This was a vicious and unprovoked attack by Brown and Akinlolu in a crowded nightclub where Brown used a glass bottle as a weapon to strike the victim's head twice.

"This kind of violence is entirely unacceptable, and the Crown Prosecution Service will work tirelessly - with the police and partners across the criminal justice system - to pursue cases like this, and prove that no one is above the law."

Brown and Akinlolu entered their pleas at Southwark Crown Court on Friday in a hearing that took less than five minutes.

Judge Tony Baumgartner scheduled the sentencing hearing for the affray charges for both men for 26 October.

The judge set bail conditions that allow Brown to leave the UK, but he must return on 25 October.

Brown is known for tracks including Loyal, Look At Me Now and With You.

He waved at fans as he arrived at court, flanked by security guards while wearing a beige suit and baseball cap.

Fans played his music, held up signs and shouted his name, with one heard declaring: "I love you Chris."

At earlier hearings, he was ordered to pay a £5m security fee as part of his bail conditions, which also allowed him to go on a world tour as long as he surrendered his passport on arrival in each country.

Last summer, the performer joked on-stage about his "nice" time in jail following his arrest in Manchester as he kicked off his tour at the city's Co-Op Live arena.

"Thank you for coming and supporting me," he said to fans in Manchester. "And thank you to the jail," he joked, referring to a spell in custody. "It was really nice."

In 2009, Brown pleaded guilty to beating his then-girlfriend, pop star Rihanna shortly before the pair were due to perform at the Grammy Awards.

He was sentenced in that case to 180 days' community labour and five years' probation.

He later said he felt like a "monster" and the fight would "haunt me forever".

Entertainment.title: Letters written by young pre-Smiths Morrissey up for auction
Entertainment.text:
Letters written by a young Morrissey before he formed The Smiths are to go to auction where they are expected to sell for £22,000.

The archive of letters, written to Birmingham pen friend, Simon Pitt, who would go on to become the city's poet laureate, by the singer between the ages of 14 and 20, includes one in which Morrissey says "my ambition is to be a rock 'n' roll star or an actor, or a writer".

Another letter dated a number of weeks later adds: "I always said I was a genius, but nobody listened."

The letters, written between 1974 and 1979, are expected to fetch a combined £22,000 estimate when they go on sale in London.

They are being offered as separate lots in Before The Smiths: The Morrissey Letters, which will be held at Dawsons Auctioneers on 26 August.

The period documented in the letters was featured in the 2017 biopic England Is Mine, which follows the young singer, whose full name is Steven Morrissey, as he struggles to find his place before forming The Smiths with guitarist Johnny Marr in 1982.

In the letters, Morrissey also speaks about seeing The Sex Pistols at Manchester's Lesser Free Trade Hall in June 1976, which he says changed his opinion on the band.

In the letter, he says: "As for the Pistols... they were pathetic. I take back all that I've said about the Pistols... They are just plain bad. Period."

He also speaks about meeting Patti Smith, along with Johnny Thunders and Jerry Nolan of the New York Dolls - the band whose UK fan club Morrissey was the president of.

Morrissey speaks of visiting New York punk club CBGB's and attempting to join The Clash, and becoming the vocalist with Manchester punk band The Nosebleeds - his first experience fronting a band.

In the letters, he says of his experience with the band: "I'm in showbusiness... I'll spring on this unsuspecting world yet...

"One thing I won't do is record for the sake of it... I'm all set for superstardom. But then, I've always been a star, haven't I?"

Morrissey also speaks about politics in the letters and his dreams of moving to America.

One letter following Margaret Thatcher's election as prime minister in 1979 reads: "Did you vote? Labour, I hope? God knows what tortures that miserable Thatcher has prepared for us woikin' class folk. I dread to fink."

The final letter sees Morrissey reveal he has joined a band in London who "have a recording contract and all that rubbish".

Peter Mason, auctioneer and senior valuer at Dawsons, said: "What struck me most was just how funny Morrissey is.

"Running through almost every letter is a wonderful sense of humour and genuine warmth that makes him an incredibly endearing character.

"Alongside the wit and unmistakable literary voice that would later become synonymous with Morrissey, the correspondence also captures Britain at a fascinating moment in its cultural history.

"Through his observations on punk, music, politics and everyday life, the letters offer a vivid snapshot of the changing British music scene and political landscape during the 1970s while documenting the emergence of a remarkable young talent long before the rest of the world knew his name."

With The Smiths, who were completed by Marr, bass player Andy Rourke and drummer Mike Joyce, Morrissey was one of the pioneers of British indie rock in the 1980s.

They achieved three UK top 10 singles, and were best known for songs such as This Charming Man, Heaven Knows I'm Miserable Now, and How Soon Is Now?

Entertainment.title: Decoding Charli XCX's new album, Music, Fashion, Film
Entertainment.text:
Charli XCX was supposed to be taking a break.

Her sixth album, Brat, was the sort of record you could genuinely call era-defining, without being accused of overstating its significance.

Experimental but accessible songs like Guess, Apple and 360 propelled the star to new heights of fame.

Her album was co-opted into Kamala Harris's 2024 presidential campaign, and Collins English Dictionary updated its definition of Brat, to acknowledge its use as an adjective characterising the music's "confident, independent, and hedonistic attitude".

After a punishing year-long tour, the singer accepted a few acting roles, wrote the soundtrack to Emerald Fennel's adaptation of Wuthering Heights and married her longterm partner George Daniel.

But instead of settling down, she found herself back in the studio.

"Out of the blue, inspiration struck me," she says. "I suddenly felt like I had something to say, so I ran with it."

In a matter of weeks, she dashed off 11 short, guitar-based songs that tried to make sense of her whirlwind two years.

The resulting album, titled Music, Fashion, Film, is smart, self-referential, funny, antagonistic and crammed full of moments to stimulate your inner earworm.

Significantly, deliberately, it's not Brat 2.0.

"If I'd made another album that felt more dance-leaning, it would have felt really hard, really sad," she told Vogue in the first interview for the album, external.

"To be boring is to die right there on the spot," she added in a newsletter to fans, external. "Give up, give in, go home, stay home, end it all."

As a result, there's a lot to uncover in the music and lyrics. Here's what we learned.

In the aforementioned Vogue article, Charli played the interviewer a track called Rock Music, featuring the lyric: "I think the dancefloor is dead, so now we're making rock music".

The publication took that as gospel, calling Music, Fashion, Film the star's "rock reinvention".

Fans recoiled. Courtney Love accused Charli of being a troll. Madonna captioned a photo, "If your dance floor feels dead, maybe you're playing the wrong music."

But while guitars are the album's predominant sound, it's far from being a rejection of club music. Even the song Rock Music is full of manipulated vocals and electronic flourishes.

"I never said I was making a rock album," Charli posted on Instagram, explaining that the song was really about her relationship with the Brat album.

"I've made electronic-leaning music for over a decade," she told music YouTuber Nicky Reardon. , external

"That's shaped who I am as an artist. [Rock Music] is kind of about my pivot from that as an artist who doesn't want to continue to do the same thing over and over and over again."

Rather than a picture of Charli, the album is being promoted with a stylish black-and-white photo of Velvet Underground musician John Cale, fashion designer Marc Jacobs, and film director Martin Scorsese.

The trio epitomise excellence in their respective fields - reflecting the album's overarching theme of art, excellence and immortality.

The photo was taken in New York this April, by Scottish filmmaker Aidan Zamiri, who's been behind the camera for some of Charli's recent music videos, as well as her mockumentary The Moment.

"Honestly it was a really emotional day," the singer told BBC 6 Music's Nick Grimshaw, external.

"I was like, 'Wow, these three people mean so much to me personally as an artist'. And I couldn't believe that they were all together, you know?

"We were so nervous and then when it was happening it was just honestly really sweet."

On Rock Music, Charli admits that the head-banging physicality of the Brat tour ended up giving her nerve damage in her neck.

"It really impacts a lot on my sleep habits," she told Sam Murphy on the Pop Pod, external, saying the pain had got "progressively worse over the past couple of years".

"When I think about touring this record I do think I should probably be taking a different approach," she added. "But who knows where I'll end up on that front, you know? Sometimes I just can't stop myself."

Fans got a glimpse of how things might change at a secret show in London last week, where Charli performed some of her new material for the first time.

Flanked by a tight, three piece band, the set was less demanding from a body-slamming perspective, without sacrificing the energy of the music.

Reviews weren't allowed - but let's just say the new material, with its distorted guitars and punchy drums, sounded even better live.

Charli's new songs find her grappling with whether she can stay true to her pugnacious, subversive roots while enjoying commercial success and personal happiness.

The slinky single SS26 discusses the pressure on pop stars to do and say the right things.

Lyrically, Charli disavows cigarettes and writes sincere apologies for her past mistakes. She even talks about using her politic as a "press strategy", noting that her part-Indian heritage "could give me quite the USP".

Laced with sarcasm, it highlights the idiocy of holding celebrities to unattainable standards, instead of letting music (and fashion and film) explore the darker side of human nature.

"If you're on the internet, there's this feeling like you need to be on the right side of every single conversation," Charli told Nicky Reardon.

"You can't just be good. You have to be the right type of good, in a specific way and if not, you're a bad person who actually had a sinister motive this entire time. So the song is actually talking about my experience with that."

Equally compelling is the single Wink Wink, where Charli emphasises her newfound maturity - wearing trousers, driving sensible cars - before admitting it's all a pose.

"I'm not a bad girl anymore / Wink, wink."

But the most nakedly honest lyric comes on I'm Afraid - potentially the least romantic song ever written about getting engaged.

"Happiness came in a box," Charli says of the proposal, before spiralling into a panic about who she'll become if she says "yes".

"I'm a wife, I'm a kid / I'm destroyed, I'm a bitch / I'm too drunk, I can't sleep / I can't feel, I'm afraid / I'm nothing without him / What if I ruin it?" she sings, as discordant synths rip apart the sonic fabric.

Connecting the songs is the idea that everyone's flawed - but the mess and the friction make life more interesting.

If the lyrics on Brat were direct and unembellished, Charli's new album takes minimalism to an extreme.

The seventh song, Yeah, is a textbook example of tension and release in pop music - that strips the idea down to its most elemental form.

For the first 30 seconds, Charli simply repeats the phrase, "I don't wanna," over and over while a guitar chugs in the background.

Then, just when you're about to hit the off switch, she declares: "Wait! Now I wanna feel it," and the music explodes into life.

It's so stupid and basic, and yet it scratches a tried-and-tested musical itch with such precision that you have to admire its audacity.

Yeah is the most demo-like song on a 29-minute album that occasionally feels under-cooked. But the brevity was quite deliberate.

"I wasn't like, 'Oh, I must make an album with tiny songs'," Charli told Nick Grimshaw.

"That was just the way that the songs came out. It was just a choice that felt right for the music that we were making."

Charli is an avowed film buff, whose fifth album was named after David Cronenberg's notorious body-horror film Crash.

The Canadian director is also the last voice you hear on Music, Fashion, Film, in an excerpt of an "hour-long" conversation he had with Charli last year,.

"What's crazy is he actually spoke in tune with the song, without ever having heard it," she told Australia's Triple J radio station., external

In the clip, Cronenberg talks about the legacy of art, and whether longevity really matters.

"Yes, some artists have created art that has really survived for thousands of years, and that's fantastic," he says. "But experientially, for them, they are dead. They are gone. They're not experiencing that."

That's not a cause for sadness, he insists. It means you shouldn't be burdened by the success (or failure) of your work.

"Oblivion is freedom."

It feels like he's showing Charli the escape route from post-Brat expectations. On the evidence of this album, she's already made it through the door.

Entertainment.title: Black Panther star Chadwick Boseman's family in legal dispute with his widow
Entertainment.text:
Chadwick Boseman's brothers are taking the late US actor's widow to court over her handling of his multimillion-dollar estate.

Derrick Boseman and Kevin Boseman have filed a petition with a Los Angeles court to force the Black Panther star's widow, Taylor Simone Ledward, to distribute money to family members, and to have her removed as controller of his estate.

They claim she has mishandled distribution of the funds and "cannot be trusted with the continued administration of the estate".

Boseman died at the age of 43 in 2020, four years after being diagnosed with colon cancer. He is best remembered for playing the lead role of T'Challa, king of Wakanda, in Oscar-winning 2018 Marvel blockbuster Black Panther.

According to court documents seen by BBC News, Boseman had assets worth $3.8m (£2.9m) but died without a will.

A court decided that 50% should go to Boseman's widow, who was also appointed the estate's administrator, with 25% to each of his parents.

The actor's brothers filed the court petition last week on behalf of their parents, Leroy and Carolyn Boseman.

The petition said Ledward "has still not distributed the estate" and "continues to exert unilateral control" over it.

Ledward is also accused of creating a "lack of transparency" around his assets, and of keeping the actor's parents "in the dark" about the deals and operations of a company that was set up to manage his image and rights.

The brothers claim Ledward's "misconduct is causing ongoing harm" to Boseman's elderly parents and depriving them "of financial assets at a vulnerable age when such support is most critical".

"Moreover, the needless continuation of these proceedings denies Decedent's [Boseman's] family closure and causes emotional distress," the court filing said.

"Imagine flipping through the channels and stumbling on a film starring your deceased son or brother, knowing that someone you do not know or trust is profiting from his image without your input or consent."

Ledward - an R&B artist who uses the name Sahn - started dating Boseman in 2015 and they got married just six days before the actor's death in August 2020.

The BBC has asked her lawyer for a comment.

In a statement to US media, the late actor's brothers said: "On behalf of our parents, we are committed to ensuring that transparency, accountability, and respect guide the resolution of these matters.

"Our hope is that this process brings clarity, honors the court's orders, and ensures the responsible stewardship of Chadwick's legacy.

"We love our brother, and we remain committed to preserving his legacy with dignity, integrity, and respect."

Entertainment.title: Fake or Fortune: BBC programme uncovers 'enormously important' 18th Century painting
Entertainment.text:
An "enormously important" 18th Century painting by the Scottish artist Katherine Read has been uncovered by the BBC's Fake or Fortune.

The portrait was brought to the programme's team wrapped in a sleeping bag, and is now thought to be worth more than £100,000.

Retired accountant Mary-Louise Wedderburn explained the painting was left to her in her uncle's will two decades ago.

Wedderburn said she had always believed the portrait may have been painted by Read, a distant relative of hers who specialised in portraying women and children.

The portrait features an Indian woman in a formal pose, wearing a string of pearls, a large emerald pendant and a nose ring.

Speaking in the episode, broadcast on Thursday, art historian Charles Greig described it as "one of the trickiest paintings I've ever had to consider".

"On the basis of all the evidence put together, I am entirely certain that this painting is by Katherine Read."

After being told of the work's authenticity and the projected value, Wedderburn said: "It's wonderful, it's unbelievable. Thank you so much.

"It's just so important to me that it's by Katherine Read, because of the family connection, but also because of who she was."

She added: "The more that we find out about Katherine Read, the more I think she was just a wonderful woman, she was just super."

Read, a well-known portraitist at the time, studied in Europe, moved professionally in elite circles and was so successful that she was paid more handsomely than her better-known contemporaries, including Gainsborough.

However, like many other female artists, she was largely forgotten, as fashions changed and some of her portraits were re-attributed to male artists.

The Fake or Fortune team authenticated the painting by trying to find other Read works to compare it to, trawling through family archives, speaking to experts and gathering letters and wills that brought fresh insight into Read's life in India.

They pieced together the story of the people she may have painted in Chennai in India, known then as Madras, including the Nawabs of Arcot, the local Mughal rulers.

Explaining his analysis, Greig said: "The evidence from the dossier that to me was the strongest was the technical analysis done by the Courtauld.

"The similarity of the portrait of [her niece] Helena Beatson: the pigments, the modelling of the figures, the brushwork, were very conclusive."

The work is thought to be the earliest recorded painting of an Indian sitter by a European female artist.

Greig noted: "One of the most interesting things about this painting is that I'm pretty certain that she [the sitter] is a member of the Nawab's family in Madras.

"That is extremely unusual because most of the other portraits of Indian ladies are a companion, or sometimes a wife, of a European.

"But I can't think of another portrait of an Indian lady of this period that is actually part of a royal court rather than a European's household. That makes it enormously important."

Art dealer and presenter Philip Mould said: "What a wonderful result, I'm sure we're going to see more works by this pioneering woman artist in India coming out of the woodwork."

Presenter Fiona Bruce added: "If, as Mary-Lou wants, it can be in an exhibition, in a gallery, where the whole world can see this picture, Mary-Lou will have given this woman not only a voice, but she will be seen.

"In a sense she will be brought to life and I think that's just a brilliant result."

Entertainment.title: King and Queen emerge from Tardis to open Glasgow Commonwealth Games
Entertainment.text:
King Charles and Queen Camilla emerged from a Tardis at the start of a spectacular Commonwealth Games opening ceremony in Glasgow.

The royal couple drew gasps and cheers from the audience at the Hydro as they appeared on a stage that had been turned into a giant garden.

Flags from 74 nations and territories were carried into the arena during the event, which also featured the Loch Ness monster and performances from Nathan Evans, Tom Walker and KT Tunstall.

The show celebrated the story of Glasgow - from its industrial past to its vibrant nightlife - ahead of a Games that will see 215 medals awarded across 10 sports.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and First Minister of Wales Rhun ap Iorwerth were among the dignitaries in the royal box for a show that lasted two hours and 20 minutes.

Glasgow, which hosted the event in 2014, stepped in to stage it for a second time after the Australian state Victoria pulled out due to soaring costs.

Although on a smaller scale to previous editions, the 23rd Games will see a record 47 para-sports events.

In a surreal opening scene, six-time Olympic champion Sir Chris Hoy emerged from the Tardis to cheers before he was, to the audience's surprise, followed by the King and Queen.

It is not the first time a monarch has made a memorable entrance to a major sporting event's opening ceremony.

Queen Elizabeth II famously took part in the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, appearing to skydive into the stadium from a helicopter with James Bond actor Daniel Craig, after he escorted her from Buckingham Palace.

After the royal couple took their seats an 18-strong Royal Scottish National Orchestra Youth Chorus entered, stood among the garden paths, and sang God Save The King.

Then, for the first time in Commonwealth Games history, the athletes took centre stage by parading into the arena before the ceremony fully got under way.

The African nations led the way with Botswana the first to enter the Hydro.

The segment was titled Ceud Míle Fáilte - Scottish-Gaelic for "a hundred thousand welcomes".

This year there was no baton relay across the Commonwealth but each of the 74 nations and territories was given a wooden baton to decorate.

As they entered, the team's baton bearer handed the baton to one of three gardeners on stage.

It is was then planted on stage to create a colourful garden.

The soundtrack, by Skye-based Valstos, fused trad and electronic music and mixed in samples from the country's musical traditions.

Organisers said it was designed to be "a symbol of common ground, bringing a piece of every nation and territory into a shared celebration of the natural world that connects us all."

The last baton was brought in by Team Scotland, who received the loudest cheer of the night as they were led in by Alex Marshall - who has won five Commonwealth gold medals in bowls - and judo champion Sarah Adlington.

After the parade, a piper appeared in a spotlight and played a single note.

The Loch Ness monster appeared on screen before being magically coaxed on to the stage by Outlander star Sam Heughan.

Pipers and drummers, including in the upper decks of the arena, delivered a rousing rendition of Flower of Scotland.

The focus then switched to a day in the life of the host city, with a dance section featuring the famous Glasgow Central Station clock.

People mimicked the 10 sports that will be played during the Games.

Nathan Evans - who shot to fame with his sea shanty Wellerman in 2021 - entered and began to sing with the Saint PHNX Band.

The song took over the station scene like a flash mob and unleashed the joy of its message: Scotland is a place called home.

Three city guides then told the story of Glasgow, using staging inspired by Scotland's pioneering textile industry and the River Clyde's shipbuilding heritage.

The city's legendary nightlife was celebrated with a section that paid tribute to venues such as the Barrowland Ballroom and the Sub Club.

Singer Callum Beattie then appeared - flanked by dancing silver unicorns and stars - and sang Scotland's unofficial football anthem, Yes Sir, I Can Boogie by Baccara.

Team Scotland got to their feet and soon athletes from every nation were showing off their best dance moves in a moment to remember.

Dr Donald Rukare, president of Commonwealth Sport, told the audience the "extraordinary legacy" of Glasgow 2014 had made the "reimagined Games" possible.

The Ugandan - who was wearing a Wallace tartan kilt in his country's colours - thanked those who had made the multi-sports event possible.

He added: "For the next 11 days, 74 nations and territories, thousands of athletes and supporters, and countless cultures and stories come together, united by one simple idea: that sport has the power to bring people together.

"In a world that can sometimes feel divided, that matters more than ever."

After the speeches, a choir hummed a stripped-back arrangement of The Proclaimers' anthem I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles) as footage of the King's Baton Relay was shown on the giant screen.

Scottish singer-songwriter Nina Nesbitt performed an acoustic version of the famous track as phones lit up the arena.

The King's Baton was then paraded around the Hydro by swimmer Hannah Miley and para-cycling great Neil Fachie.

The baton was finally passed to professional basketball player Kieron Achara, who handed it to the King.

The monarch then removed a message he had placed in the baton in March last year - 500 days before the start of the Games.

King Charles said a key theme of the relay had been raising awareness of plastic pollution and the damage it causes to marine life.

He told the audience: "I extend my warmest gratitude to the city of Glasgow, all the athletes, organisers, volunteers and all those who have made this event possible."

In between, she channelled the energy of the Tartan Army from the World Cup by leading the crowd in a a chant of "No Scotland No Party".

Nathan Evans and the Saint PHNX Band then replayed the beat of their hit Home, as they returned to the stage.

The finale involved a giant pyrotechnic Teacake taking off from the centre of the stage.

This was a nod to the dancing Teacakes which provided one of the most memorable moments of the 2014 opening ceremony at Celtic Park.

As one of the biggest global gatherings the city has seen came to end, it was impossible not to feel uplifted.

The hope for these Games is that the best is yet to come.

Entertainment.title: Meta glasses banned by Comic-Con promoter after 'secret filming'
Entertainment.text:
The promoter behind some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK has banned Meta glasses from its events to stop "secret filming" of guests and attendees.

Monopoly Events said a number of guests had told the company they would be reluctant to appear at Comic-Con shows again after cases of recordings taking place without their knowledge.

The ban is applicable to Meta glasses and any other "wearable recording devices".

Attendees caught using the devices will be asked to leave the convention, but some fans on social media warned the move could negatively affect disabled attendees.

Devices like Meta glasses feature an almost invisible camera in the frames, with small speakers in the arms.

Wearers can record video or take a photo by touching the frame - usually activating a light on the glasses in the process.

In a social media statement, Monopoly Events said: "After a consultation period we can no longer permit the wearing of any recording device at our events.

"The vast majority of the talent and agents at our events felt that these were a violation of their privacy and were damaging and spoiling the interactions at the tables. Several expressed concerns that they might not continue to attend in-person events if they were being recorded in secret.

"We had similar feedback from event attendees, many of whom are not comfortable with the knowledge that other convention goers might be filming them without consent.

"Anyone seen using one of these devices might be asked to leave the event and forfeit any unfulfilled autographs or photographs they had purchased. Please let's make these events a safe space for everyone."

However others raised concerns about the impact on disabled people. One wrote: "Have you considered how this will affect disabled people and how that affects you under the Equality Act? Many people in the blind and partially-sighted community use them to safely navigate surroundings and be able to attend the event."

There was also scepticism from some fans regarding how enforceable a ban would actually be.

Female attendees at comic conventions have previously spoken out about suffering harassment and unwanted attention from other people while there.

Earlier this week the ferry operator CalMac paused bridge visits on its vessels after a passenger used "smart glasses" to film without permission.

The man was caught filming passengers and crew using Meta glasses.

Entertainment.title: Actress Jaime Winstone joins Strictly Come Dancing 2026 line-up
Entertainment.text:
Actress Jaime Winstone, known for roles in Made in Dagenham and EastEnders, has joined the line-up for Strictly Come Dancing 2026.

She is the eighth celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner and Dani Dyer.

Winstone, who won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition.

The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me".

"I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"

Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.

She has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.

After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year.

Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:

Known as Great Britain's most successful Paralympian of all time, Dame Sarah Storey has secured 19 gold medals across the nine Paralympic Games she competed in.

The swimmer and cyclist said embarking on the challenge is "hugely exciting" and she "can't wait to get started".

"I have always loved watching Strictly and my daughter Louisa is a very talented dancer, so to be able to learn from the best and hopefully understand even more about her world, is incredibly motivating!" she said.

The former athlete won four golds at London 2012. She started her career as a swimmer and later switched to cycling, winning 30 Paralympic medals in total.

Best is known for hosting Big Brother with AJ Odudu on ITV since 2023, and as host of the Hits Radio Breakfast Show alongside Fleur East and James Barr.

He said it was "an absolute dream" to be taking to the BBC One contest's dance floor in September, "albeit a pretty terrifying one".

Best added: "I've been lucky to do lots of live telly before, but absolutely nothing like this. And I cannot wait!

"I have no idea if I can actually dance, but bring on the sequins, bring on the quicksteps, bring on the dance floor! I'm going to try to enjoy every minute of it."

Mercer was part of the winning couple on ITV dating show Love Island last year, and also works as a model and DJ, and is an ambassador for a young people's mental health charity.

"I have grown up watching the show with my family and am so excited to now be part of the cast," he said.

Mercer also showcases his Afrobeat, hip-hop and street dance moves on his social media accounts.

"Dancing is a huge passion of mine and I can't wait to learn ballroom and do the foxtrot for the first time!" he added.

Delta Goodrem is also part of this year's celebrity list, with the Australian singer and actress becoming the third celebrity to be announced for the upcoming series.

"I've been incredibly honoured to perform on many different stages throughout my career - from TV, theatre, film sets, to touring my own shows around the world," Goodrem said.

"There is, however, one stage I've never stepped onto and that is the ballroom floor. I'm absolutely thrilled to be joining Strictly and can't wait to get started."

She rose to fame in hit Australian soap opera Neighbours and recently represented her nation in the 2026 edition of the Eurovision Song Contest.

Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton is also part of this year's line-up.

Appleton, best known for his work with Kim Kardashian, joins singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem, EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and reality star Dani Dyer in the battle for the Glitterball trophy.

The Leicester-born Color Wow creative director said: "I'm thrilled to be joining Strictly Come Dancing and coming home to the UK for this incredible experience."

He has also created red carpet looks for the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, while having his work showcased on the covers of publications including Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Vanity Fair.

"I've always believed that the best things happen when you take a chance and try something new," added the 43-year-old, who this year released a memoir entitled Your Roots Don't Define You.

"I may know my way around a salon floor, but the dance floor is a whole different story - and I can't wait to get started."

Lacey Turner was the first contestant to be announced for this year's series, which is expected to begin in September.

She said she was "so excited to be making my way to the dance floor", adding that she was a "huge fan" of the show.

Turner, 38, is best known for her role as Stacey Slater on the BBC One soap, which she joined in 2004.

She has won a British Soap Award and National Television Award for her role, and has also starred in TV dramas including the BBC's Our Girl.

In a video posted on Instagram, Turner said she was "so excited and so terrified at the same time" to be taking part in the show.

"But I've had so many friends do Strictly, and I thought it was about time that I pluck up the courage and made my way on to the dance floor."

Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.

The first line-up announcements were made significantly earlier than usual - the BBC usually confirms the line-up in August.

Speaking to ITV's Good Morning Britain in June, Ballas said: "There are going to be some people on there that will make you go 'wow'."

Asked about the new presenting trio, Ballas said she was "very excited to see what they bring" to the show.

"I know they took lots of chemistry tests, as did everybody, and those chemistry tests have brought those three people together, and I believe it's absolutely unbelievable," she said.

Ballas described the number of new elements on this year's show as "quite extraordinary", but added that it will still feel familiar to viewers.

"I don't think they'll change the show too much, maybe tweaks here and there, but no major changes."

Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.

Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.

However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

Entertainment.title: The perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and more
Entertainment.text:
It is important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and challenging you’ve been meaning to get round to for ages will make you feel guilty and more liable to give in to scrolling, and if you take too many supposedly upmarket “must reads” of the summer, you will simply prove to yourself just how much overhyped averageness there is out there, when all you want is something satisfying.

You need to be able to chop and change depending on your mood, which means fiction and nonfiction. And finally, you need to be able to throw all of these rules out of the window if you find a sandy old water-stained copy of, for example, James Herbert’s Domain in your holiday cottage and decide to devote yourself to 600 pages of post-nuclear mutant rat-strewn London, or choose to go for a full-on Maeve Binchy sesh.

My top tips for this summer? For the outward journey: Kathy Burke’s smash-hit and brilliant autobiography A Mind of My Own, a reminder of the absolute Britishness you are leaving behind. For that first post-rosé afternoon when you are filled with warmth and benevolence towards the world and everyone in it: Whistler by Ann Patchett.

For a wonderful immersive epic where everyone is also extremely boiling hot all the time: This Is Where the Serpent Lives by Daniyal Mueenuddin. For cruising altitude day four when everyone else has gone to see some stupid boring hot cave and left you alone and you want something quality and capable of being finished in an afternoon: Glorious Exploits by Ferdia Lennon. For the day everyone is doing your head in: Emma Cline’s huge hit from a couple of years ago, The Guest, a thoroughly nasty piece of work and the best of all those “neighbourhood psycho” books.

Nonfiction palate cleanser day: OK, everyone is going to be reading the Maggie Haberman Trump book, but for the love of God could we possibly not think about him for one solitary five-second interval? That would be the definition of a holiday. If annoying Americans are still your bag, try Belle Burden’sStrangers, about a seemingly perfect, rich Wasp marriage unexpectedly going down the toilet.

For queueing at non-EU passport control and cursing Nigel Farage’s £5m: The Impossible Fortune by Richard Osman. Forget the motley crew of celebrity impersonators that squelched along in his wake; Osman’s lightness of touch and genuine comic ability means this slips down more easily than free limoncello. Bonnes vacances!

author of The Housemaid

One of my favourite reads of the year has been TheCalamity Club by Kathryn Stockett. I’ve been on a historical kick lately, and this novel set in the southern US during the Great Depression is historical fiction at its best. The audiobook is masterfully narrated and by the last chapter, I had tears in my eyes.

author of Yesteryear In The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson a group of friends in their mid-30s in a tight-knit Massachusetts coastal town deal with secrets, romance and the fallout from a stunning betrayal. It’s frothy and clever and perfect for a vacation.

Taffy Brodesser-Akner

author of Fleishman Is in Trouble I brought Here in the Dark by my New York Times colleague Alexis Soloski on vacation a couple of years ago. I couldn’t put it down from the minute I started it, even missing a family dinner so I could continue reading. (Sorry, kids!) It’s a modern noir about an acerbic theatre critic who finds herself caught up in a mystery, and I can’t say enough about its voice, its humour, its darkness, its poignancy and the twists and turns that make it a truly original thriller. I loved it.

author of Heartstopper

Convenience Store Woman by Sayaka Murata is about a woman whose only dream is to work at a convenience store and, like much of Murata’s work, explores the inner world of a woman who feels deeply uncomfortable about the role she’s forced into by society. It’s short, it’s strange, it’s the perfect read for a trip away this summer – and a great introduction to Murata, if you haven’t dipped in before.

author of the Slough House series

Beaches are for walking along not reading on, but when the paddling’s done and a sand-free environment’s been found, Daniel Mason’s Country People is a treat. A failed academic and his family relocate to Vermont, where his PhD avoidance strategies involve increasingly alarming immersion in local folklore. An absurd, joyful delight.

author of The Maid

The Paper Palace by Miranda Cowley Heller. August heat, a summer cabin in Cape Cod, and the unravelling of one woman’s secrets. Elle is happily married with three kids, but her whole life is upended by an illicit encounter with a childhood friend. A charged generational saga about love, desire and loss – you’ll need regular dips in the water to cool yourself as you read.

author of None of This Is True

The best page-turner I’ve read this year is It’s Not What You Think by Clare Mackintosh. She already lays claim to one of the genre’s greatest twists in her 2011 hit I Let You Go and here Mackintosh is back to deliver multiple twists, short chapters and non-stop reveals in this scintillating read.

author of Call Me by Your NameLondon Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe is about a 19-year-old Londoner who desperately wants to join the world of super-wealthy Russian oligarchs, many of whom live in the capital. He manages to affect belonging to that class until he is finally exposed for who he really is – a smart, resourceful but hapless kid. The story is totally addictive, real, and I couldn’t put it down.

author of The Guest List

The Wedding People by Alison Espach is an absorbing, transporting book that left me with a serious what-to-pick-next panic after finishing it. I took it on holiday last year and the summer setting makes it perfect: the waterfront hotel, the excursions on boats and in open-top cars, and also the unfurling sense of optimism. It’s a paean to solo travel, to leaving it – quite literally in this case – all behind. But it’s also a book with teeth, poignancy, depth and humanity, all qualities I look for in a top-notch summer read.

author of The Night Stairs

The Pinnacle by Abir Mukherjee is a satirical thriller set in a Mumbai skyscraper. A washed-up American actor is accused of killing his Bollywood starlet wife. It’s got everything you could want from a book: belly laughs, unforgettable characters, a thumping plot and simmering political rage.

author of the Ninth House series

The Last Baron by Tom Sancton. Thick with loathsome individuals and rich with history, this heavily researched story of a 1970s kidnapping in Paris spans generations. It is wildly juicy, just be prepared for a Succession experience: you’ll struggle to find anyone to root for but you won’t be able to look away.

author of The Midnight Library

The Infinite Sadness of Small Appliances by Glenn Dixon is a weird, wonderful book about a vacuum cleaner that becomes sentient after hearing To Kill a Mockingbird read aloud. Said vacuum cleaner renames herself Scout and embarks on a quest to save the human she lives with. It’s highly original and feels like a sign that – in the age of AI – the way out is through vivid human creativity.

author of The Names A will-they-won’t-they romance is a much-anticipated holiday treat for me, and Annabel Monaghan’s are guaranteed to make my cheeks ache from smiling and keep me reading until 2am. In Nora Goes Off Script, screenwriter and single mum Nora falls for a leading actor when her house is co-opted as a film location.

author of Conclave Graham Greene has accompanied me on a lot of holidays over the years, especially the novels set in hot climates. I recommend in particular The Power and the Glory, The Honorary Consul and The Quiet American – perfect reading for a sweltering beach, a deserted baggage hall, or a night-time veranda with a sickly blue light zapping the insects.

author of Yellowface

I recently read and loved Anthony Doerr’s Cloud Cuckoo Land. Like David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas, it’s a testament to ridiculous hope and the power of stories that is also ridiculously, formally ambitious – its crosscutting storylines span centuries and continents. It’s precisely the kind of book I needed to remind me how high human storytelling can soar.

author of On We Go

An MP has been murdered and a taunting message left in binary code: “Catch me if you can.” So begins Body of Lies, the politically and technically prescient conclusion to Jo Callaghan’s unique Midlands-set series featuring Kat and Lock, a human and AI detective pairing. Brimful of big ideas and heart, its action-packed finale is, to put it mildly, as moving as it is thrilling.

author of Claws Out!

The Enchanted April by Elizabeth von Arnim. I read this recently and found it completely charming and brilliantly transporting. Four women, bored, lost, lonely and miserable respectively, take a villa in Italy for a month of respite. It’s funny, tender and trots along at pace. But above all else, it’s a novel about women and the community that springs up between them. A perfect beach read.

author of American Wife

Crash Into Me by Robinne Lee is the ideal beach read not just because I literally was reading it on the beach earlier this week, though I was, or because the American cover features waves crashing on the sand, but because it’s an irresistible mix of glamorous, thought-provoking and sexy. Jamaican-born, New York‑raised, France-dwelling photographer Cecilia is living temporarily with her famous director husband and kids in LA when she reconnects with Anouk, a model with whom she had a complex encounter 20 years earlier. Now the two women are middle-aged and equally tempted to protect and blow up their lives. This is Lee’s follow-up to The Idea of You, and it’s just as juicy.

author of Witch Trial

Nonesuch by Francis Spufford is an absolute banger. Historical meets fantastical in this London blitz-set novel. The perfect combination of literary and compulsive page-turner, it reads like a dream. A bonus recommendation for Time to Burn by Ellery Lloyd, which also starts in the blitz but adds a thoroughly contemporary, compelling time-travelling twist.

author of The Burning Grounds

My choice is The Shadow Step by Mark Billingham, the latest in the Blackpool-set series featuring the wisecracking, ballroom-dancing detective Declan Miller. This one sees our hero running an investigation into the murder of a rather despicable young man, which quickly gets derailed by the kidnapping of a student. As with the others in this series, Billingham weaves a fiendish plot but also lets rip with the jokes. An absolute joy to read.

author of The Death of Us

I’d recommend Main Characters by Bobby Palmer. Seb and Clara meet in a Soho square, and an epic on-again, off-again romance begins. But their story is narrated by everybody except the main characters. Sometimes it’s a close friend, but we also hear from people‑watchers, neighbours and colleagues. The result has the feeling of a short-story collection, with small, perceptive insights into a vast cast of characters, and the ways lives collide and divert. Make sure you have sunglasses to hand – I wept.

author of The Barbecue at No 9

This year, Dead Heat by Sabine Durrant exceeded my unofficial “beach read” criteria of 1) page-turning crime or thriller 2) set in hot weather. This elevated psychological thriller, which takes place over a Greek summer, gave me serious Patricia Highsmith vibes. It’s classy, cinematic and truly thrilling.

author of Getting Away With Murder In Five by Ilona Bannister, someone on a London train platform will die in five minutes when the train arrives. As the clock ticks down, you meet the characters who might die, and you get to know them intimately. If you want a completely immersive read, this is for you.

author of Karla’s Choice If Lewis Carroll sat down with Mick Herron to write a thriller about memory and nightmare, you’d get There Is No Antimemetics Division by qntm. A funny, gripping and genuinely disturbing counter-espionage monster novel told in beach-friendly episodic style. What’s not to love?

author of The Girl on the Train

Four Terrible Parents by Calla Henkel. Careering towards 40, two rock stars, an artist and a former banker decide the time has come to settle down, get married, and co-parent a child (while also renovating a hotel in South Carolina). Henkel’s comedy-slash-thriller is so fiendishly plotted you might not even notice all she has to say about art, love, friendship and family.

author of The Map of Bones

Recently reissued, Fenny by Lettice Cooper – first published in 1953 – is a coming-of-age story set in the Tuscan hills. Dripping with heat, the sound of cicadas and the smell of the pine trees, this is the story of a Yorkshire governess who pitches up at a villa outside Florence in the years before the second world war and falls in love with the country, the light, the Italian pace of life. Heartwarming, atmospheric, a perfect summer read.

author of Just My Luck

Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth. You may not have heard of this Australian-born, New York Times bestselling author yet, but I’ve been reading her for years; I love everything she’s written and I’m waiting to see her to blow-up here. Her bittersweet, thrilling dramas are shot through with life-enhancing humour. Somehow Hepworth’s Aussie sunshine floods off the page even when she’s delivering dark twists and murders. In this novel, unapologetically grumpy, fiercely independent 81-year-old Elsie lives quietly in an Australian suburb, except everywhere she goes people die in mysterious circumstances.

author of All In I couldn’t get enough of Some Bright Nowhere by Ann Packer, which is told from the perspective of a husband whose terminally ill wife asks him to move out so her best friends can move in. The literary equivalent of a friend telling an increasingly shocking story, it’s an unexpected and deeply moving read.

Entertainment.title: Euphoria gave me the courage to come out to my friend – now we’re together
Entertainment.text:
I don’t remember the exact moment when I started catching feelings for my friend Ellen. It might have been when she trusted me to cut her hair into a feathered bob, or when I noticed she’d taken to keeping my favourite tea at her parents’ house. But in the summer of 2019, a month before our final year of school together, I realised I was falling in love.

We were 17 at the time and had been best friends since our first year of high school, both of us part of the same tight-knit group of girls. Ellen and I knew each other well and were quick to make each other laugh, but we were also very different. Whereas Ellen is reserved and gentle, I’m loud and loquacious. So my sudden attraction to her was confusing – especially since neither of us was openly queer.

I had been raised in an accepting, liberal household in Stockholm, where queerness was never frowned upon. And yet, I had always assumed that I was straight. It was the default script that had been handed to me. So, each time Ellen greeted me with her one-dimpled smile, I tried to ignore the fluttering in my chest, thinking it would be too complicated, too daunting. Even as I sensed those feelings might be mutual, I didn’t dare act on them. I was worried it might damage our friendship.

This all changed when I watched the first season of Sam Levinson’s television show Euphoria. Set in suburban California, the show (an adaptation of an Israeli series of the same name) follows a group of high-schoolers as they recklessly navigate adolescence. They abuse drugs, drink alcohol, have sex, watch porn and fall in and out of love.

More specifically, it was the relationship between Rue (Zendaya), a recovering drug addict, and the town newcomer, a transgender girl named Jules (Hunter Schafer), that drew me in. The two meet after a party at the end of the first episode and quickly forge a connection. As their friendship deepens, Rue begins to fall for Jules.

I recall watching the first few episodes at a friend’s house and being enthralled by Rue and Jules’s plotline, and how tender and complex it was. Even though my own world was far removed from the dark, gritty one of Euphoria, I related to the more innocuous parts of their story: the insecurities Rue has about her feelings toward Jules, that flicker of hope each time the line between platonic and romantic love is blurred. It all felt so similar to what I was experiencing.

There was also something refreshing about the depiction of the characters’ sexuality. In the series, there are no major coming-out scenes, no need for Rue or Jules to explain their orientation. When Rue tells her mother she’s in a “relationship” with Jules, her mother simply responds by saying: “It may not matter what I think, but I really like her.” This is not to say that coming-out scenes in fiction aren’t important. But for me, Euphoria was the first show that portrayed queerness as liberating – and it helped me realise I could feel that way too.

Watching Rue and Jules open up to one another gave me the push I needed; when I finally did kiss Ellen, she kissed me right back. And as morning light filtered through the blinds of her bedroom, I knew I had made the right decision.

We have been together for six years. We didn’t settle into a relationship right away; we needed time to figure out coupledom. But slowly, Ellen and I have managed to build a life, furnished with our mutual love of books, movie nights and laughter. She is my bulwark and the person who helps me decompress.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Police investigate donations by Richard Tice company to Reform UK
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Police are investigating payments to Reform UK by a company controlled by the party's deputy leader, Richard Tice, BBC News has learned.

Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of £250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election, when Tice was party chairman.

Tice has said the money was given to his firm by Fiona Cottrell, a significant donor to Reform UK and mother of a convicted fraudster with close links to Nigel Farage.

Tice said: "This is the first I have heard of it - if true why are the Met Police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties? Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?"

Earlier this month, the Times newspaper, external revealed that two donations given directly by Fiona Cottrell to Reform UK in May 2024 were being investigated by the Metropolitan Police.

That investigation relates to legislation governing elections, which bans concealing or disguising donations derived from an "impermissible" donor, or the use of "false" information about a donation including the amount or the identity of the donor.

The BBC has asked Fiona Cottrell for comment.

Britain Means Business, which is solely owned and controlled by Tice, received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.

Disclosures to the Electoral Commission show that the company then donated a total of £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.

Tice told the BBC earlier this month that it was entirely his choice for the company to give half of the money from Fiona Cottrell to his party.

The payments came to light when the Guardian newspaper, external revealed they had been flagged to the National Crime Agency as part of its Suspicious Activity Reports programme.

Now BBC News has learned that they are part of the Met's investigation into donations to Reform UK.

The BBC understands that the party was not aware of the investigation into the payments from Britain Means Business.

A Reform UK spokesman said: "Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far."

All four payments were made in the weeks before the general election on 4 July 2024, when Farage and Tice were first elected to Parliament:

The first direct donation, external from Ms Cottrell of £250,000 appeared in the party's accounts on 9 May

The second, external, also £250,000, appeared a few weeks later on 29 May, just over a month before polling day

One payment, external from Britain Means Business of £250,000 was made on 10 June

Another payment, external from Britain Means Business of £250,000 was made on 12 June.

Tice was chairman of Reform UK until 11 July, having previously been its leader. He then became deputy leader.

Records of all the donations have been published by the Electoral Commission.

Records on the Commission's website show Reform's bank account was frozen in the weeks before the election.

Other notes on the site suggest the account was first frozen a maximum of nine days after Britain Means Business's second donation.

It is not known why the account was frozen.

A spokesperson for the Electoral Commission said it was aware that the Met had issued a statement about an ongoing police investigation and it had no further comment to make.

The Met investigation into all four donations has been ongoing for more than a year.

Asked about the donations from Britain Means Business, the Met repeated a statement originally issued earlier this month after The Times's investigation.

A spokesperson said: "An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan Police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK General Election."

They added: "Detectives from the Met's Special Enquiry Team are investigating alleged offences under Section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.

"Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made.

"An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police."

Fiona Cottrell's son, George Cottrell, has been at the centre of a political row in recent weeks.

The Sunday Times has reported he supported Farage by paying for staff and security before the 2024 election, but these benefits were not declared once Farage became an MP. Farage has since stepped down as an MP and is standing for re-election in the constituency of Clacton.

Farage has consistently argued any money given to him before he was elected an MP came in a personal capacity and therefore did not need to be declared. Lawyers for Cottrell have said he "categorically disputes allegations and assertions made by The Sunday Times, which clearly fail to reflect what that publisher was told in advance of its reporting".

Asked by the Sunday Times if Cottrell had transferred money to his mother before she made donations to Reform UK, his lawyers at Carter Ruck said: "Our client has confirmed his instructions that any donations by his mother have been entirely her own decision."

George Cottrell has long been a close political and personal ally of the Reform UK leader.

He pleaded guilty to fraud in the United States and spent eight months in jail there, before being released in 2017.

Upon his release he moved back to the UK and now lives in Montenegro.

At a rally in Norfolk on Tuesday Nigel Farage said he had "absolutely no idea" whether George Cottrell had given money to his mother to donate onwards to the party, adding, "What's it got to do with me how families sort out their finances?"

"If the money was hers legally and she gave the donation, I don't see what the problem is," he said.

Britain Means Business was set up in August 2017 under the name Leave Means Leave and campaigned for a "clean Brexit".

The organisation was set up by Tice and John Longworth, a former boss of the British Chambers of Commerce and prominent Brexit campaigner.

Longworth left Leave Means Leave in January 2020, the month the UK officially left the EU.

A few months later Tice changed the organisation's name to Britain Means Business. He now solely owns and controls the business.

BreakingNewsTab.title: More than 300,000 evacuated as wildfires rage in France and Spain
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Firefighters are struggling to contain wildfires in south-west France as strong winds push flames towards the city of Bordeaux, with one official saying they "are far from having the fire under control."

More than 300,000 people in France and Spain have fled fires which have been raging for days, as winds and high temperatures hamper efforts to contain them.

In Spain, where a state of emergency has been declared, a change in weather conditions has helped firefighters outside Madrid.

Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez admitted there were "complex times ahead". Meanwhile, authorities in València confirmed the death of a man in a fire.

The man, believed to be in his 70s, was found dead in his car by firefighters as they extinguished a fire in the Salt de l'Aigua ravine in Manises, according to local media reports.

In France, a further 55,000 were ordered to evacuate late on Saturday, taking the total to around 250,000 people in south-western regions of Gironde and Landes regions.

Firefighter Captain Nicolas Braz told AFP news agency that the fire had created "its own winds - complete with whirlwinds", adding it was "erratic and unmanageable".

It is set to be another "difficult night," he said.

France has mobilised its military to help with the response and extra reinforcements from the army have been sent to help firefighters by clearing brush and creating fire breaks.

President Emmanuel Macron said France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed".

A British couple holidaying in Bordeaux said they noticed the flames get worse on Friday night, as the fire approached.

"At about seven o'clock you could smell smoke. We thought someone was having a barbecue," Maisie told BBC Newsbeat from their holiday rental.

Her partner, Caleb, said the ash has now covered the pool in the house and turned their feet black when walking outside.

The smoke "really hits your lungs right away", they added.

Nearby, in Saint-Aubin-de-Médoc, residents evacuating said the situation was "stressful", with one local describing it a "disaster".

The final leg of the Tour de France, due to take place Sunday, has been shortened from 133km (83 miles) to 89km (55 miles) so that security forces can be redeployed to areas affected by wildfires, organisers and police have said.

Macron is set to have an emergency meeting with ministers as 30 or so fires rage across the country - a situation which the government said is totally unprecedented.

She said fires had started earlier in the year when, in April, the Netherlands activated the EU's civil protection mechanism which triggers support and reinforcements from other countries.

Lahbib told the BBC: "Last year, one million hectares burned during the summer and so we are expecting to face another historical, sad record because the season has started earlier in the year."

She also warned that more outbreaks are likely as the summer goes on.

"Forecasters are predicting, unfortunately, another heatwave so we can expect other wildfires," Lahbib added.

France has activated the civil protection mechanism and will receive water bombers, comprising three Canadairs planes from Croatia and two Air Tractors from Portugal, as well as Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and 40 members of a Romanian forest fire team.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said 11 planes and helicopters have also been sent to France and Spain from the EU's firefighting fleet.

Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield, BBC Your Voice and Srosh Khan, BBC Newsbeat

BreakingNewsTab.title: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."

Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".

His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11, is still coming to terms with having seen the flames.

"Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."

He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August.

"It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."

David Morton, a headteacher, had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun.

But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning.

"Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," the 53-year-old said.

"We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."

He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."

The family, from Gloucestershire, has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.

Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.

Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."

She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.

While the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.

Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries.

"I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans.

"But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."

In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.

But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.

Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.
